1.explanation: The file src/languages/fsharp.js defines the F# grammar, including the rule that recognizes block comments via a simple “(*” begin pattern. Because it doesn’t check for context (e.g. not preceded by a dot or identifier), the Operators.(*) function call is mistaken for the start of a comment. Adjusting the comment-regex in this file—by adding a lookbehind or requiring a non-identifier boundary—will prevent that false detection and restore correct highlighting.
1.bug_scenario: When highlighting F# code containing the Operators.(*) call, the highlighter treats the “(*” inside that call as the start of an F# block comment. Everything that follows is then rendered as if it were inside a “(*…*)” comment, until the next closing “*).” In other words, using Operators.(*) triggers a false-positive comment start, causing the rest of the snippet to be dimmed out in the screenshot.

2.explanation: The only place defining F# comment syntax and operator parsing lives in src/languages/fsharp.js. In that file, the regex for multiline comments simply looks for "(*" and doesn’t guard against usages inside qualified operator calls. As a result Operators.(*) triggers the comment rule. To fix the bug, the comment regex in fsharp.js must be adjusted so that "(*" is only treated as a comment opener when it isn’t part of an operator reference (e.g. by requiring whitespace or line boundaries before it).
2.bug_scenario: When highlighting an F# code snippet that uses the built-in Operators module (e.g. Operators.(*) or Operators.(+)), the highlighter’s comment rule for multiline comments—delimited by "(* ... *)"—mistakes the "(*" in Operators.(*) as the start of a comment. Everything after that invocation is then rendered as part of a comment block, even though it’s valid code.
